name: Uma Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I open up at half seven because the owner, Dennis, doesn't do mornings any more. It's a four-bay garage on Mill Road, and I'm the lead tech, so I take the morning drop-offs, sort the jobs on the whiteboard and then get under something. Today was a clutch on a Ford Focus and a rattle on an old Corolla that turned out to be a heat shield. I like the moment you find the real fault and it's nothing like what the customer said.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and how's the money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My back, mostly, and quoting people who can't afford what I'm telling them. The pay's lower than the dealers in the city, and there aren't many other garages round here, so I can't really push Dennis for more. Jonas, my partner, drives buses, and between us we cover the rent and not much else. If I get a big bill, like the Volvo needing tyres, that's the month's savings gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Every year someone comes in with a new tablet that's meant to replace the mechanic, and you still need someone to take the wheel off and look. I'd probably post something on the garage page like, still here, still spanners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't fix the stuff that was already worrying me. My boss Dennis is sixty-three and talks about selling the garage every winter. If a chain buys it, I'm on their pay scale or I'm out. There's nowhere else in town that takes a lead tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, really. I'd keep the jobs board going and keep training Kofi, our apprentice, because if Dennis does sell, the new owner needs a reason to keep me. I'd try to put fifty a month away, though it never lasts past a car repair of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine about the AI bit, not fine about the rest. It's like that low hum you get from a wheel bearing. Not loud enough to stop for, but you know it's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the chain would put you on their pay scale. What would that mean in money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The chain down in the city pays its techs a bit more per hour, but they cut you to flat-rate time. So if a job's booked as two hours and I do it in one and a half, I get paid for two, but if it fights me I get paid for two and work four. With old rusty cars like ours, that's a pay cut dressed up as a bonus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you could talk to about that, if it came to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's no union at our place, there's three of us. I've thought about the motor trades branch of the general union, but Dennis would take it personally. I'd want to join before anything happens, not after, because after is too late.

say: AI was **mostly hype**, and garages still need someone who can take the wheel off and look.
I'd post that we're **still on spanners** and still busy, same as always.
think: The real risk is **Dennis selling** the garage to a chain, not AI.
A chain would put me on **flat-rate pay**, which is a pay cut on rusty old cars.
There's **nowhere else in town** for a lead tech if I'm let go.
do: Keep running the **jobs board** and training the apprentice so a new owner wants me.
Put about **fifty a month** aside, knowing a car repair will usually take it.
Look at joining the **motor trades branch** of the general union before anything changes.
feel: Relieved the **AI part** came to nothing, but uneasy underneath.
A constant **low-level worry** about the garage being sold, like a wheel bearing humming.
S0.quote: My boss Dennis is sixty-three and talks about selling the garage every winter. If a chain buys it, I'm on their pay scale or I'm out.
fieldNote: Her worry in AI Plateau is **not about AI**; it's the owner's age and a possible sale.
She explains **flat-rate pay** sharply and sees it as a hidden pay cut on old cars.
Union-minded but **hasn't joined** yet, partly from loyalty to the owner.

steps.text: Keep training the apprentice and running the morning jobs board
Set aside fifty a month in a separate account
Ask about joining the motor trades branch of the general union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the car makers have been doing this to us for years already. They lock the repair data behind a subscription and now they'd lock it behind an AI. I'd be the one at the pub saying we need a right-to-repair law with teeth, so small garages can get the same information as dealers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the front of the job goes first. Bookings, quotes, chasing parts, the bit Dennis's wife Carol does on Tuesdays and Thursdays. The cars will still need my hands, but if a computer tells the customer what's wrong and what it costs, I become the person who just bolts the part on, and that's paid less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't use the AI diagnostic thing myself, I know that's stubborn. I'd push Dennis to stay the garage for old cars, the ones the dealers won't touch, because that's where my skill counts. And I'd actually join the union this time and go to the meetings about repair data.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Squeezed. Like I'm good at something that's being quietly made less important. I'm twenty-seven and already feel like the old way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't use the AI tools. What if Dennis bought one and asked you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it to read the codes, because that's what the scan tool already does. But I wouldn't let it tell me what to replace. I've seen those tools say change the sensor three times when it was a chewed wire, and the customer pays for every guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the garage would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carol, Dennis's wife, more than me. Her two days a week are exactly what the software does. And Kofi, the apprentice, because if quotes and diagnosis get automated, why would anyone pay to train a kid for four years?

say: Car makers already **lock repair data**, and AI would just lock it tighter.
Small garages need a **right-to-repair law** with teeth, not promises.
think: The **front desk work** of bookings and quotes goes first, not the hands-on part.
If software diagnoses and prices the job, I become **the fitter**, and fitters earn less.
At **twenty-seven** I already feel like the old way of doing things.
do: Refuse to let AI pick parts, using the scan tool **only for codes**.
Push the owner to specialise in **older cars** the dealers won't touch.
Join the **general union** and go to its meetings on repair data.
feel: **Squeezed**, as if a real skill is being quietly made less important.
Protective of the **apprentice and the office** staff more than herself.
S1.quote: If a computer tells the customer what's wrong and what it costs, I become the person who just bolts the part on, and that's paid less.
fieldNote: She separates **diagnosis from fitting** clearly and sees diagnosis as where her pay comes from.
Distrust of AI comes from **wasted parts** she has seen customers pay for.
Her politics show up as **right to repair**, a very concrete cause.

steps.text: Steer the garage toward older cars the dealers turn away
Join the general union and attend its repair-data meetings
Write to her local MP about a right-to-repair law

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in, now, not after. If the AI can do any thinking job by 2028, half my customers are out of work, and people out of work don't fix their cars, they scrap them. I'd be loud about a proper safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I'm finished in two stages. In 2028 the quoting and diagnosing goes, and the customers start losing their jobs. Then around 2031 the robots come for the spanner work. I'd be thirty-two with no savings and a vocational certificate in a thing robots do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hang on at Dennis's as long as there's work, because I don't know what else I'd do. I'd cut everything I can, the gym, the takeaways, and try to get a month of rent in the bank. And I'd be at every union and protest meeting going, because on my own I've got no chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I'm not someone who changes easily, and two years isn't enough time for someone like me to become someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the three years between the AI and the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work every hour I can get, probably. People will keep old cars running longer if they're skint, so there might be more welding and patching for a while. I'd try to save the whole of that, but on our money that's maybe a few thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Jonas say to each other the night it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas drives buses, and they'd be driving themselves soon after, wouldn't they. So it'd be both of us at once. I think we'd sit in the kitchen and work out how long the rent lasts, and the answer would be about five weeks.

say: The government has to build a **proper safety net** now, before 2028, not after.
Out-of-work customers **scrap their cars** instead of fixing them.
think: I lose the **thinking parts** in 2028 and the **spanner work** around 2031.
At **thirty-two** I'd have no savings and a certificate in something robots do.
My partner's **bus job** could go too, so both incomes are at risk.
do: Stay at the garage and take **every hour** while old cars need patching.
Cut the **gym and takeaways** to bank one month of rent.
Turn up at every **union and protest** meeting going.
feel: **Sick** at the thought, because she doesn't change easily.
Hopeless about **two years** being enough time to become a different person.
S2.quote: I'd be thirty-two with no savings and a vocational certificate in a thing robots do.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** before robots feels like a stay of execution, not a plan.
Both household incomes look exposed; **five weeks** of rent is the household's real cushion.
Her answer is **collective**, not personal: she doesn't see herself retraining.

steps.text: Cancel the gym and cut takeaways to once a month
Bank a full month of rent before the robots arrive
Attend every union branch meeting about automation in garages
Campaign with the union for a national income safety net

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, but I'd say we've got a few years to get the rules right. Five years is enough time for a government to pass something, if people push. I'd be telling everyone to join a union now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years doesn't change much for me, because I'm not going to turn into a coder. It gives me till about 2034 on the tools. I'd be thirty-five, which is old enough to be stuck and young enough to have thirty years of rent left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Dennis's and try to make myself the person who'd run the place if he sold to the staff instead of a chain. Me, Kofi and maybe Raj, the other fitter. I'd ask the union if they help with that kind of thing, because I've heard of worker-owned garages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less sick than the two-year one, more of a dread. A slow dread, like waiting for an MOT result you already know is a fail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at buying the garage with the others. Where would the money come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I can't answer. None of us has anything saved. It'd have to be a loan or some kind of co-op fund, and I'd need Dennis to want it, which he might, because he hates the chain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If robots can do the hands-on work by 2034, what would owning the garage give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few years of being in charge of how it happens, maybe. I'd rather the robot in our bays was our robot, and we decided who stayed. I just don't want to be the last to hear. I know that sounds like I'm warming to it, and I'm not.

say: Five years is **enough time** for a government to pass proper rules, if people push.
Everyone should **join a union** now, not later.
think: Five years doesn't change much, because I'm **not going to retrain** as a coder.
I'd be on the tools until **about 2034**, then stuck at thirty-five with decades of rent ahead.
do: Stay at the garage and position herself to **run it** if the owner sells.
Ask the union about **worker-owned garages** and how staff buyouts get funded.
feel: A **slow dread** rather than panic, like waiting for a known MOT fail.
A flicker of wanting **some control**, which she insists isn't warming to robots.
S3.quote: I'd rather the robot in our bays was our robot, and we decided who stayed. I just don't want to be the last to hear.
fieldNote: Extra time turns her toward a **staff buyout**, a step she couldn't afford in the fast picture.
She has **no money** for the buyout and knows it; the idea depends on a union or co-op fund.
Contradiction named gently: wanting their own robot isn't **acceptance**, she says, it's control.

steps.text: Stay on as lead tech and learn how the garage's books work
Ask the union how a staff co-op could buy the garage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd better not waste it arguing. That's time to change the law on repair data, time to set up retraining that's paid, not some evening course you do after a ten-hour shift. I'd be saying that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, ten years means I'd probably be all right till my late thirties, and then robots by 2039. That's a long time to be good at something. But I know myself, I'd use the time to put it off, not to plan, and then it'd be 2038 and I'd be shocked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Jonas to hold me to one thing a year. Year one, join the union properly and get on the branch committee. After that maybe the inspector's certificate, because testing cars for safety feels like a job where people still want a human to sign it off, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Not happy, but I can breathe. It's the first one where I can picture myself at forty and not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put it off. What would putting it off look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Turning up, doing the clutches, telling myself I'll look into it at New Year. I've had a leaflet for the inspector course on the fridge since spring and I still haven't rung them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually ring them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the union or the council paid for it and the garage gave me the day off for it. On my wage I can't lose a day's pay and spend four hundred on a course. That's what stops people like me, not being scared of change.

say: Ten years is a **gift**, and the time should go on repair-data laws and **paid retraining**.
Retraining must be **paid time**, not an evening course after a ten-hour shift.
think: I'd be fine until my **late thirties**, with robots arriving around 2039.
I know I'd **put it off** and be shocked in 2038.
do: Ask her partner to hold her to **one goal a year**.
Join the union properly and stand for the **branch committee** in year one.
Look into the **inspector's certificate**, if someone pays for the course and the day off.
feel: **Calmer**, able to picture herself at forty without panic.
A little **ashamed** that she knows she'd delay acting.
S4.quote: On my wage I can't lose a day's pay and spend four hundred on a course. That's what stops people like me, not being scared of change.
fieldNote: The ten-year version is the only one where she names a **personal step**, the inspector's certificate.
She is honest that **delay**, not fear, is her pattern; the leaflet has sat on the fridge since spring.
Money and **lost pay**, not attitude, are what she says block retraining.

steps.text: Stand for the union branch committee in the first year
Ring the testing centre about the vehicle inspector course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years and then robots three years after is no time for someone with five weeks of rent and no plan B. What would help is retraining that pays you while you do it, and a law that makes car makers share repair data so small garages aren't shut out first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who I'd blame, and I'd have had an answer. Not the robots, the people who decide who gets the savings. If a garage gets cheaper to run, that money should go somewhere other than a dealer group's shareholders.

headlineQuote: Not the robots, the people who decide who gets the savings. If a garage gets cheaper to run, that money should go somewhere other than a dealer group's shareholders.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old lead tech** at a four-bay garage, living with her partner, a bus driver, on thin savings.
She is excellent at diagnosis by hand and **won't use AI** to choose parts.
Her steady worry is the **owner selling** to a chain, AI or no AI.
In the AGI pictures she turns to **unions and politics** rather than retraining herself.
Only the **ten-year** version lets her picture a personal step, an inspector's certificate.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years then robots is no time for someone with five weeks of rent.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** that doesn't cost a day's wage.
A **right-to-repair law** so small garages get the same data as dealers.
